content: An asymptomatic carrier is an individual who harbors an infectious disease or possesses an abnormal gene associated with a recessive genetic disorder but does not exhibit any symptoms of the condition. Despite not being affected themselves, these individuals can transmit the disease or genetic disorder to others. One historical example of an asymptomatic carrier is Mary Mallon, famously known as Typhoid Mary. She was a cook in New York City during the early 20th century and unknowingly carried the bacterium responsible for typhoid fever. Several cases of typhoid fever were traced back to her by the Health Department, as she transmitted the infection to members of the families she worked for, despite not falling ill herself. At the time, there was no method to eliminate the disease from carriers, so authorities attempted to restrict her from working as a cook to prevent further spread of the infection. Another example involves the daughters of Queen Victoria, Princess Alice and Princess Beatrix, who were asymptomatic carriers of the X-linked hemophilia gene. This gene, specifically an abnormal allele necessary for producing one of the blood clotting factors, was passed on to their descendants. Their male offspring who inherited the gene developed hemophilia, a condition characterized by impaired blood clotting, while their female offspring were carriers who could pass the gene to approximately half of their children. This genetic transmission contributed to the spread of hemophilia within the royal families of Spain and Russia through intermarriage. The genetic term for this type of carrier status, where a recessive trait is carried without being expressed, is referred to as being a heterozygote.
